strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: synthetic data generation for right-censored survival datasets, where preserving covariates, event times, and censoring is practically useful for clinical ML.

The proposed model is a plausible and relatively simple extension of mixed-type tabular diffusion, adding joint generation of covariates, event indicators, and observed times together with a Cox-style survival objective.

The empirical section compares against relevant tabular and survival-specific baselines, including SurvivalGAN and TabDiff, across three public medical survival datasets with multiple metrics and 10 random seeds.
The paper provides useful implementation detail in the appendix, including datasets, hyperparameters, hardware, and additional downsampled-data experiments.
weaknesses: The central claim that the method preserves the censoring mechanism is not directly supported. The evaluations mostly measure covariate distances, TSTR survival prediction, Kaplan-Meier MSE, and RMST gaps, but do not report censoring-rate fidelity, conditional censoring distributions, event-time versus censoring-time decomposition, or calibration of censoring conditional on covariates.

The proposed survival loss is not clearly or rigorously justified for generative modeling of censored data. It is a discriminative Cox partial likelihood term applied to denoised covariates, and it only uses uncensored events directly. This does not obviously ensure correct joint generation of event indicators and observed times, especially under informative or covariate-dependent censoring.

There appears to be a technical error in the Cox loss formula: the denominator is written as a sum over exp(r_i) rather than exp(r_j) for j in the risk set. If this is implemented as written, the loss is wrong; if it is a typo, it still weakens the method presentation. There are also smaller notation inconsistencies, such as using I_{dcont} while diffusing z=(x_cont,T).

The claimed advantage over TabDiff is mixed. TabDiff is competitive or better on several key survival-specific metrics: in Table 7 it has better RMST gap on AIDS and METABRIC and much better KM MSE on GBSG2; in Table 3 it is essentially tied or better on METABRIC downstream metrics. This weakens the argument that the survival-tailored loss consistently improves survival fidelity.

The manuscript claims ablation evidence against naive tabular diffusion, but there is no clean ablation isolating the survival loss, censoring/event modeling choices, sparsity weighting, adaptive lambda calibration, or administrative censoring. Comparing to TabDiff as a full baseline is not enough to establish which design component matters.

Evaluation protocol details are insufficient. It is unclear whether generative models are trained only on a training split before TSTR evaluation or on all real data, which raises possible leakage concerns. Preprocessing, split construction, synthetic sample size, metric aggregation across downstream models, and hyperparameter selection procedures are not fully specified.

The work does not address privacy or memorization risk, despite motivating synthetic clinical data as a way to train models without direct access to patient-level data. There is no membership inference, nearest-neighbor, duplicate, or disclosure-risk analysis, and no substantive research ethics discussion.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the model is largely TabDiff-style mixed-type diffusion plus a Cox-style auxiliary loss. This may be useful, but the paper overstates novelty and significance relative to the amount of new modeling insight and evidence provided.

Presentation is generally readable, but there are several grammatical issues, awkward claims, and overstatements. The discussion of limitations is essentially absent, and the conclusion claims reliable preservation of censoring mechanisms beyond what the experiments establish.

strengths: The paper targets a real and underexplored problem: synthetic data generation for censored time-to-event datasets, where standard tabular generators are not obviously adequate.

The proposed model is reasonably motivated as an adaptation of mixed-type tabular diffusion, and the end-to-end generation of covariates, event indicators, and observed times is a plausible design direction.
The empirical section includes multiple public survival datasets, several generative baselines, several downstream survival models, and repeated runs with mean and standard deviation reporting.
The appendix provides useful implementation details, including dataset descriptions and many hyperparameters, which is a positive step for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim that the method preserves censoring mechanisms is not convincingly supported. The evaluation reports covariate distances, TSTR C-index/Brier, KM MSE, and RMST gap, but does not directly evaluate censoring distributions, censoring conditional on covariates/time, event-vs-censor calibration, or informative/non-informative censoring behavior.

The survival-tailored loss is only weakly connected to the generative objective. It is a Cox-style risk loss on denoised covariates, while event time and censoring are otherwise treated largely as ordinary generated variables. This does not establish that the learned joint distribution over covariates, event times, and censoring is correct.

There are apparent methodological ambiguities and possible errors. In the Cox loss denominator, the manuscript writes a sum of exp(r_i) over the risk set rather than exp(r_j), and key quantities for the sparsity-aware weighting such as tau and the decay parameter are not specified in the hyperparameter tables.

The evidence is mixed despite strong wording. On survival-specific metrics in the appendix, SURVDIFF is often not best: TabDiff or SurvivalGAN match or outperform it on several RMST/KM entries. On METABRIC downstream performance, SURVDIFF is essentially tied or worse than TabDiff. These results undercut claims of consistent superiority and faithful event-time preservation.

The experimental protocol is underspecified in ways that affect soundness. It is unclear whether generators are trained only on training folds before TSTR evaluation or on all real data, which could create leakage when downstream models are tested on real outcomes. Preprocessing, feature handling, train/test splits, model selection, and statistical testing are not described in enough detail.

The baselines are not fully convincing. The paper emphasizes SurvivalGAN as the main tailored baseline, but also relies heavily on generic tabular baselines without carefully adapting or diagnosing them for censoring. There is no ablation isolating the survival loss, sparsity weighting, censoring indicator generation, or administrative censoring step in the main experiments.

The privacy and ethics treatment is inadequate for a medical synthetic-data paper. There is no memorization, membership-inference, attribute-inference, or disclosure-risk analysis, even though the stated motivation includes sharing patient-level synthetic data.

Presentation is polished at a high level but overclaims relative to the evidence. The manuscript repeatedly states that SURVDIFF preserves censoring mechanisms and achieves state-of-the-art performance, while the reported metrics and appendix show a more limited and sometimes inconsistent picture.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: synthetic data generation for survival analysis with right censoring, where generic tabular generators are not obviously appropriate.

The proposed method is conceptually sensible: it extends a mixed-type tabular diffusion backbone to jointly generate covariates, observed time, and event indicator, and adds a survival-aware Cox-style objective.

The evaluation includes relevant baselines, including SurvivalGAN and TabDiff, and uses both fidelity metrics and train-on-synthetic/test-on-real downstream survival metrics across three public medical datasets.

Empirically, SURVDIFF performs strongly on the main downstream metrics, especially C-index and Brier score, and generally improves over SurvivalGAN. The small-sample sensitivity study is also useful and clinically relevant.
The manuscript is mostly clear and well organized, with implementation hyperparameters and dataset descriptions provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Some central claims are overstated. The supplementary survival-specific metrics are mixed: TabDiff is better than SURVDIFF on RMST gap or KM MSE in several settings, so the claim of consistently superior survival fidelity is not fully supported.

The treatment of censoring is somewhat shallow. The model generates an observed time and event indicator jointly, but it does not explicitly model latent event times and censoring times or distinguish administrative from informative censoring except via a post-hoc note. This limits the strength of the claim that it preserves the censoring mechanism.

The survival loss formulation has a concerning apparent error: Eq. 10 uses exp(ri) in the denominator sum rather than exp(rj), which would make the Cox partial likelihood incorrect as written. If this is only a typo, it should be fixed; if implemented literally, it would materially affect soundness.

The methodological novelty is moderate. Much of the architecture follows TabDiff, and the main addition is a Cox-style auxiliary loss plus weighting. This is useful, but not a major conceptual advance unless the censoring mechanism is characterized more rigorously.

The evaluation is limited to three public datasets, all relatively standard. There is no stress test on known synthetic survival-generating processes where the true event-time and censoring distributions are known, which would directly test whether the method recovers censoring mechanisms.

Privacy and ethics are underdeveloped for a clinical synthetic-data paper. The manuscript motivates data sharing, but does not evaluate membership inference, attribute disclosure, nearest-neighbor memorization, or differential privacy tradeoffs.

Reproducibility is only partial: hyperparameters and datasets are listed, but code availability, preprocessing details, baseline tuning fairness, and exact train/test splitting procedures are not sufficiently specified for confident independent reproduction.
Presentation has minor issues, including grammatical errors, some awkward claims, and reliance on t-SNE visualizations that are visually suggestive but not strong evidence.
